newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OLYMPICS-SAMARANCH PLANS TO BE IOC PRESIDENT UNTIL 2001.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-SAMARANCH PLANS TO BE IOC PRESIDENT UNTIL 2001.

text.p: Juan Antonio Samaranch, who has turned the Olympics from a troubled sporting showpiece into a billion-dollar business, wants the most powerful job in the Games movement until 2001.

Samaranch, who turns 77 in July, announced on Wednesday that he would stand again for re-election as International Olympic Committee (IOC) president later this year and bid for a fourth term in one of the most significant positions in sport.
If he wins, the Spaniard, who has a reputation as a diplomat as well as a shrewd businessman, has the chance to complete 21 years in office after taking over the job in 1980.

But Samaranch, who has a chance to continue at his age only because his Latin allies in the organisation managed to force a vote to raise the IOC age limit in 1995, said he would be in charge for the last time at an Olympic Games in Sydney in the year 2000.

"It was not a difficult decision. I like what I do. It is not a sacrifice to be president of the IOC," Samaranch said after the IOC announced that its four vice-presidents were putting his name forward to the vote at the IOC's session in September.
"If I am re-elected I will be very pleased, if I am alive, to go to the Games in Sydney. They will be my last Games for sure."

Samaranch has played a huge role in turning the Olympic movement into a successful commercial outfit and on Wednesday signed a television deal for more than $2 billion with the American network NBC for the 2004 and 2008 Summer Games and 2006 Winter Games.
He has said for a while that he would carry on if his health was in order, and he is not expected to face opposition in the election.
If he completes his fourth term in office, Samaranch will be 81 by the time the next election takes place in 2001. But his age does not seem to be a problem within the organisation.

"I don't see anybody running against him," said IOC vice-president Dick Pound, who was once seen as heir-apparent to Samaranch and voted against the raising of the age barrier at the Budapest meeting in 1995.
"He said to us, 'Look I'm 77 and in good health. If at any time in the middle of my mandate I do not feel physically capable of carrying on then I'm out of here'."
Samaranch is regarded as sport's leading diplomat who is regularly seen shaking hands with heads of states around the world.

He has not had life all his way in the last few years, however. In the memorable Budapest vote the IOC turned down three alternative plans to remove the then 75-year-old limit which would have stopped him from seeking a new term now.

But later in the session, Samaranch's Latin allies calmly made a suggestion to raise the limit again, went for another vote, and won when IOC members were unwilling to incur the chief's wrath a second time.
